1. Vasa Museum
The only preserved 17th-century warship in the world. The Vasa sank on her maiden voyage in 1628, was raised in 1961, and now fills a purpose-built hall — 98 percent original wood, 64 meters of carved Baroque ambition, the most visited museum in Scandinavia.

From Hotel: 11 min · 6 min → Nationalmuseum
1. Nationalmuseum
Sweden's national museum of art and design, opened in 1866 on Blasieholmen, housing 700,000 objects spanning Swedish and European painting, decorative arts, and design from the Middle Ages to the present. After a five-year closure, it reopened in 2018 with two new gallery wings — the Treasury and Design Depot.

2. Gamla Stan
Stockholm's medieval old town — a knot of cobbled lanes, ochre and rust facades, and gas-lit corners dating to the 1200s. Anchor the wander at Stortorget, the oldest square, then drift down Västerlånggatan and find Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, the city's narrowest alley at 90 cm.

3. Riddarholmen
The "Knights' Islet" — a tiny, hushed island of 17th-century nobility palaces gathered around the cast-iron spire of Riddarholmen Church, burial place of Swedish monarchs. Evert Taubes Terrass at its western edge looks straight across the water to City Hall.

1. Royal Palace
The Swedish monarch's official residence since 1754 — a Baroque palace of 600 rooms built to replace the medieval Tre Kronor Castle. Three museums inside: the Royal Apartments and Hall of State, the Treasury with the Crown Jewels, and the Tre Kronor Museum tracing the palace's medieval origins.

2. Strandvägen
Stockholm's grandest boulevard — 1.2 km of late-19th-century stone palaces lining the north shore of Nybroviken, built for the 1897 Stockholm Exhibition. The uniform six-story limestone facades have stood unchanged since; a line of classic wooden vessels moors permanently along the quay.

10 min · 4 min → Swedish History Museum
3. Swedish History Museum
Sweden's national history museum, covering 7,000 years from the Stone Age to the Renaissance. The underground Gold Room holds 50 kg of prehistoric treasures — Migration-era gold torcs, Viking hoards, and reliquary art — making it one of Europe's richest collections of pre-medieval gold.

Sweden's largest museum of cultural history — 1.5 million objects spanning 500 years of Swedish life, from Sami culture and Viking-era artifacts to fashion, folk art, and domestic interiors. The castle-like Neo-Renaissance building on Djurgården, opened 1907, was designed to evoke a Nordic palace.

Köttbullar
Swedish meatballs with cream sauce, lingonberries, and pressed cucumber — the national comfort dish, done properly in Stockholm's classic kitchens.
Meatballs for the People · Operakällarens Bakfickan · Pelikan
Gravlax
Salmon cured with salt, sugar, and dill, sliced thin and served with hovmästarsås — the sweet mustard-dill sauce that defines Swedish cured fish.

Pickled herring in a dozen marinades, and fresh-fried Baltic herring with mash and lingonberries — Stockholm's beloved quayside classic since the sail-boat days.

Food Delivery
Uber Eats
Foreign number: accepted. — it runs on the same Uber account as the ride app, so no second code has to arrive.
Wide restaurant selection across Stockholm's central neighbourhoods; covers Södermalm, Östermalm, Norrmalm and Vasastan, with most orders delivered within 25–40 minutes. Strong on international cuisine alongside Swedish classics.
ubereats.com
Foodora
Foreign number: accepted. — sign-up runs on email, Apple or Facebook with no phone field; the mobile number is added later for courier contact and its SMS code reaches foreign numbers.
Stockholm's most-used delivery platform with the deepest local restaurant coverage — strong on Swedish lunch spots, neighbourhood pizzerias and grocery delivery from ICA and Coop. The first platform to launch in Sweden, with broad suburb coverage beyond the inner city.
foodora.se
Wolt
Foreign number: not required. — sign-up runs on Google, Apple, Facebook or email with no phone field at all, so no verification code is sent.
Helsinki-founded delivery platform with a curated restaurant selection in central Stockholm; tends toward higher-rated local spots and popular chains. Useful for quality delivery across Gamla Stan, Norrmalm and Södermalm when Foodora coverage thins.
wolt.com

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted. — the code comes by SMS to any international number, and "Call me with code" reads it out if the SMS is blocked.
Widely available ride-hailing option across Stockholm with upfront fares confirmed before booking; reliable for trips between Gamla Stan, Östermalm and Södermalm. A practical alternative to taxis when the SL network requires multiple connections.
uber.com
Bolt
Foreign number: accepted. — the SMS code often fails to reach a non-European number until you are on a European network; a local eSIM number is the fallback.
European ride-hailing alternative to Uber operating across Stockholm; fares are typically 10–15% lower on comparable routes with upfront quotes before confirmation. Worth comparing both apps for longer hops to Djurgården or the Birka ferry terminal.
bolt.eu

Day Trips by Train
Mariefred · 38 min
A storybook lakeside town beside Gripsholm Castle, Gustav Vasa's red-brick stronghold on Lake Mälaren. Ride Mälartåg to Läggesta, where the volunteer-run ÖSlJ narrow-gauge steam railway rolls you into town on century-old carriages May through September.
book at: SJ or Omio
Strängnäs · 50 min
A medieval cathedral town on Lake Mälaren — the 13th-century Gothic cathedral holds royal regalia and the tombs of King Engelbrekt and King Charles IX. The cobblestoned old town's streets descend the cathedral ridge to the lakefront harbor.
book at: SJ or Omio
Västerås · 1 hr 5 min
A Viking-age capital on Lake Mälaren — the 13th-century cathedral with Sweden's tallest spire, the Anundshög burial mounds and runestone field just outside town, and a well-preserved medieval castle on the waterfront.
book at: SJ or Omio
Nyköping · 1 hr 10 min
A quiet medieval town on the Baltic coast — 13th-century Nyköping Castle, a compact old town and a harbour waterfront, reachable in just over an hour on direct SJ trains along the main southern mainline.
book at: SJ or Omio
Norrköping · 1 hr 19 min
Sweden's industrial-heritage showpiece — a riverscape of 19th-century textile mills turned museums, concert halls, and cafés along the Motala ström rapids, with around 35 direct trains a day.
book at: SJ or Omio

Heads Up
Stockholm City Hall — Tickets Released One Week Ahead
A guided tour is the only way inside; online tickets appear just one week in advance. Gallery of the Prince closed Saturdays.
Slussen — Mega-Construction Around the Ferry Quay
The Slussen rebuild continues for years — detours around the route-82 ferry quay and metro entrances.
Kungliga Operan — Last Season Before 5-Year Closure
The Opera House closes at the end of the year for a five-year renovation — last performance December 1.
Royal Palace — Apartments Close for Receptions
The Royal Apartments can close fully or partially, sometimes at short notice, for the King's official receptions.
Worth Knowing

Where the Lake Meets the Sea

Stockholm exists because of one geographic accident: this is the exact point where Lake Mälaren pours into the Baltic. Day 1 walks that seam — City Hall stands on the freshwater side, Monteliusvägen looks over it, and the locks at Slussen have been mediating the meeting of lake and sea since the 1600s. The city's very name — log islet — comes from the timber barriers medieval Stockholmers sank at this choke point to control who sailed in.

The Vasa never made it past that meeting of waters. On her 1628 maiden voyage she sailed barely 1,300 meters — capsizing in full view of the city, roughly opposite where the Grand Hôtel now stands. Walking from the hotel to the museum on Day 2 retraces almost exactly the distance the ship managed in her entire career, which makes the 64-meter giant in the hall feel less like a relic and more like a neighbor who never left.

The Royal Palace sits on the same island as Gamla Stan — Tre Kronor Castle burned there in 1697, and the monarchy lived without a permanent home for half a century while this Baroque replacement rose in its place. Strandvägen, a few bridges north, tells the opposite story: Sweden's gilded age, not its ruins. Built in six years for the 1897 Stockholm Exhibition, the avenue's uniform limestone facades have never been replaced by glass towers — so an afternoon walking from the palace to Östermalm covers four centuries of Swedish ambition in one direction.
